lessons.title: আমি (āmi) — "I," from an old word for "we"

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: you can do this one in the car, but part of it needs your eyes. For that part you will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now. I will say so again when we reach it, but leave this section until you have stopped: The letters in this word.

segments.text: To answer "how are you?" you first need "I" — and it began as a word for "we".
আ (independent long ā) + মি (mi) becomes আমি (āmi).

আমি (āmi, "I") is not from Sanskrit asmi, "I am", though the two look alike. CDIAL lists Old Bengali āmi under asmad, the stem of the Sanskrit plural pronoun "we, us" (CDIAL 986): Bengali took an old word for "we" and made it its everyday "I", as it did with tumi, "you". Its possessive is the আমার (āmār, "my") from Chapter 3.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: "I" can often be dropped

segments.text: Bengali verbs carry the person in their ending — āchhi already means "I am" — so āmi is often left out once it's clear. You still learn it first, because the answer to kēmon āchho? begins with it.

lessons.title: কেমন (kēmon) — "how," another of the k- questions

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: you can do this one in the car, but part of it needs your eyes. For that part you will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now. I will say so again when we reach it, but leave this section until you have stopped: The letters in this word.

segments.text: You met কি (ki, "what") in Chapter 3. Here is its sibling.
কে (kē, kô + the e-sign) + মন (mon) becomes কেমন (kēmon).

কেমন (kēmon, "how, of what kind") is from the interrogative stem ka-, from PIE kʷo- — the same question-root behind English wh- and Latin qu-. Bengali's questions nearly all begin with this k-: ki (what), ke (who), kôbe (when), kōthāy (where), kēmon (how). It is the Indian branch of the same family of question-words that gave English what/who/how.
CDIAL lists Bengali ke, "who", under that stem (CDIAL 2574) but has no entry for kēmon itself, so how its ending formed is not settled.

lessons.title: তুমি কেমন আছো? (tumi kēmon āchho?) — "how are you?"

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page

You can listen to everything else now. I will say so again when we reach it, but leave this section until you have stopped: The letters in this word.

segments.text: The everyday "how are you?" — and the first time Bengali brings back a verb "to be."
The new word is আছো (āchho, "are you"), from the verb আছা (āchhā, "to be, to exist, to have") + the familiar-you ending -o. Note the ছ (chh) — a breathy ch.
তুমি কেমন আছো? (tumi kēmon āchho?) = তুমি (tumi, familiar "you") + কেমন (kēmon, "how").
আছো (āchho, "are") — "you how are?", the verb last.
All three are inherited: tumi from yuṣmad-, "you" (CDIAL 10511), kēmon on the stem ka-, āchho from ākṣēti, "abides" (CDIAL 1031).

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: now the copula returns

segments.text: In Chapter 3, Bengali dropped "is": āmār nām Arun ("my name Arun"). That zero copula works for equations (X is Y). But "how are you?" asks about a state — how you exist — and for that Bengali uses a real verb, আছা (āchhā). So: no verb for "my name is Arun," a real verb for "how are you." Respectful form: āpni kēmon āchhen? (āchhen for āpni). Match the "you" to the verb-ending.

lessons.title: ভালো (bhālo) — "well," and how to answer
lessons.gloss: well, good — and the reply "আমি ভালো আছি"

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: you can do this one in the car, but part of it needs your eyes. For that part you will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now. I will say so again when we reach it, but leave this section until you have stopped: The letters in this word.

segments.text: The word that answers "how are you?" — and one Bengalis say all the time.
ভা (bhā, an aspirated b + long ā) + লো (lo) becomes ভালো (bhālo).

ভালো (bhālo, "good, well, fine") is the everyday Bengali "good" — likely from Sanskrit bhadra ("good, auspicious, gentle"), worn down over centuries into bhālo. It is one of the most-used words in the language: bhālo lāge ("[I] like it"), bhālobāsā ("love," literally "good-dwelling").
CDIAL lists it under Sanskrit bhalla, "auspicious", which it derives from a form bhadla- beside bhadra (CDIAL 9408).
With the āchhā verb: āmi bhālo āchhi — "I am well" (āchhi = "I am/exist"). The whole exchange:
— tumi kēmon āchho? ("How are you?") — āmi bhālo āchhi, dhônnobad. ("I'm well, thank you.")

lessons.title: কোনো ব্যাপার না (kono bæpār nā) — "no matter"
lessons.gloss: it's no matter / no problem / you're welcome

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page

segments.text: When someone thanks you — or apologises — this is the easy, gracious reply, and it reuses a word from Chapter 1.
কোনো (kono, "any") + ব্যাপার (bæpār, "matter, affair" — with the ya-phola on ব্য) + না (nā, "no/not," from Chapter 1) becomes kono bæpār nā.

কোনো ব্যাপার না (kono bæpār nā) literally means "[it's] no matter" — kono ("any") + bæpār ("matter, affair") + nā ("not"). It serves as "it's nothing / no worries / never mind / you're welcome." The word ব্যাপার (bæpār, "matter, affair, business") is Sanskrit — vyāpāra ("occupation, dealing"). And না (nā) you met in Chapter 1: the ancient negative, PIE ne, behind English no, not, none. So the reply pairs a Sanskrit noun with the oldest negative in the family.

blocks.title: What you've built — roots you now carry

segments.text: kēmon from the interrogative k- (PIE kʷo-), cousin of English how/what.
āmi from Sanskrit asmi, cousin of English am.
bhālo from Sanskrit bhadra "good"; āmi bhālo āchhi "I'm well".
nā from PIE ne, English no (in kono bæpār nā).
A stranger asks āpni kēmon āchhen? — give a full, polite reply, and answer their thanks. (Āmi bhālo āchhi, dhônnobad — and to thanks, kono bæpār nā.)
